concept_edges.logic: The three assignments int t = a; a = b; b = t; exchange the values of a and b, as a trace of the variable values after each statement shows.
Java has eight primitive data types (boolean, char, byte, short, int, long, float, double); each, like any data type, is a set of values and a set of operations on those values.
A variable must be declared before an assignment can store a value into it.
A declaration pairs a type with an identifier, e.g. int count;.
Every variable is named by an identifier that follows the naming rules.
int is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for integers.
Assignment needs a declared variable on its left side to store the computed value into.
An expression can be a literal, a variable, or operations on them; we compute with a variable by using its name in an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = compares two values instead of assigning
misconceptions.correct_rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Assigns a new value to a variable declared final.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A final variable cannot be reassigned after it is initialized; the compiler reports an error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: assigning a reference copies the object
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b copies the value of a into b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes name = value; to declare a new variable.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration needs a type: type name = value;

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An int result that is too large is automatically stored as a bigger number.
misconceptions.correct_rule: int arithmetic is 32-bit; a result outside the range wraps around.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333....
misconceptions.correct_rule: Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: local variables get a default value on their own
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes Sytem.out.prinln or a misspelled variable name.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every name must be spelled exactly, including capitalization.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable can contain more than one value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"
misconceptions.correct_rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: keywords may be reused as identifiers
misconceptions.correct_rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first
misconceptions.correct_rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Statements in a program can run in any order.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: String is a primitive type like int.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Uses a variable that was never declared, or under a different name (studentTotal vs total).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every variable must be declared, and used with exactly the declared name.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value
misconceptions.correct_rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference
misconceptions.correct_rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.

levels.name: Prestructural / sensorimotor
levels.criterion: L0 for assignment: the answer holds a rule that contradicts Java.
levels.deciding_question: Does every rule the answer applies to assignment agree with the language rule? If it reads the code with everyday meanings, applies a wrong rule, or switches rules within one trace, it is L0. A slip in an otherwise rule-correct trace is L2 with an error, not L0.

levels.name: Unistructural / atom x text surface
levels.criterion: L1 for assignment: the answer states one correct rule without applying it.
levels.deciding_question: Does the answer cover every part of the code, in order, with the values (L2)? If it covers one part or only states the rule, it is L1.

levels.name: Multistructural / block x execution / preoperational
levels.criterion: L2 for assignment: the answer applies these rules to every part of the code, in order.
levels.deciding_question: Is the answer many segments mapped onto lines (L2), or one segment stating the purpose of the whole (L3)? A correct output with no value-by-value justification is not levelled.

levels.name: Relational / relations x function (concrete operational begins)
levels.criterion: L3 for assignment: the answer relates the parts by these rules.
levels.deciding_question: Was the purpose deduced from the code, or only guessed from traced input/output pairs (then L2)? Does the answer stay within the given code (L3), or reason about changed code, an error class or a new program (L4)?

levels.name: Extended abstract (concrete-operational reversibility and conservation)
levels.criterion: L4 for assignment: the answer reasons beyond the given code by these rules.
levels.deciding_question: Does the answer link the code to a broader context: a changed program, a class of inputs, an unseen problem? Re-tracing changed code value by value is L2; fixing one given failing case is L3.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression". Right rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

Points to LT (replace each variable with its current value, then apply operators in precedence order). Applied unevenly, a student substitutes current values for some variables and old or future values for others, or respects precedence in one subexpression only. (here mixing in: "a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"")
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

Adding parentheses that match the default grouping keeps the value, and rewriting with an equivalent formula (4 * (x - 3) as 4*x - 12) keeps it for ints. Changing one operand's type (3 to 3.0) can change both the result's type and its value.
wrong rule: 10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333. Right rule: Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.
wrong rule: An int result that is too large is automatically stored as a bigger number. Right rule: int arithmetic is 32-bit; a result outside the range wraps around.

Points to LT (each int operation is done immediately in 32-bit integer arithmetic). Applied unevenly, a student truncates 10 / 3 to 3 in one step but computes 10 / 3 * 3 as 10, or wraps on one overflow but not another. (here mixing in: "10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333")
Changing a variable from int to double changes / from truncating to fractional, and output from 3 to 3.0. Multiplying before dividing keeps precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98, but 59 / 60 * 100 is 0).
wrong rule: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
wrong rule: A variable can contain more than one value. Right rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Points to LT (a read gives the current value, and each assignment replaces it). Applied unevenly, a student updates the value after some assignments but keeps the first value after others, or switches between a memory model and an equation model across tasks (y = x - y read as x = 2y). (here mixing in: "a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference")
wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

wrong rule: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it. Right rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.
wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

Renaming a variable consistently keeps behavior. Reordering statements that write and read it changes results (a = b; b = a; is not a swap). Moving its declaration into a loop body narrows its scope and resets it on every pass.

wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.

Points to LT (three assignments in order, each using current values). Applied unevenly, a student traces the first two steps correctly but uses a's original value in the third, or calls one segment a swap and the other a copy without tracing either. (here mixing in: "a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values")
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.

Reordering the steps (int t = a; b = t; a = b;) breaks the swap: both variables end up holding a's value. Dropping the temporary breaks it the same way. Running the correct swap twice restores the originals, so a swap is its own inverse.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.

wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

Points to LT (a declaration runs once when reached and creates the variable, and later assignments only update it). Applied unevenly, a student re-creates or zeroes the variable on some passes but not others, or treats a declaration further down as already in effect. (here mixing in: "int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned")

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

Moving a declaration into an inner block (such as a loop body) shrinks its scope and re-creates the variable on each pass, so an accumulated value is lost. Moving it out widens its scope. Changing its type changes which values and operations are legal.
wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

Points to LT (each operation is done in its type's fixed size). Applied unevenly, a student truncates and wraps int results on one line but treats another int intermediate as an unbounded real number, e.g. tracing 59 / 60 * 100 as 98. (here mixing in: "String is a primitive type like int")

wrong rule: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned. Right rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

Switching one primitive type for another changes range and precision. int to long removes overflow up to about 9.2e18. int to double keeps fractions but stops being exact for very large integers. Changing a type to boolean breaks every arithmetic use.

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
